blocks.title: Attribution
blocks.md: The lecture slides show these figures without naming the paper; their numbering, titles and notes match Autor (2019).

1. **Cities became much more educated.** In 1970 the college share barely rose with density; by 2015 it ran from about 0.17 in the least dense to 0.41 in the densest commuting zones.
2. **Middle-skill jobs disappeared fastest in dense places.** Production, clerical, administrative and sales jobs, once concentrated in cities, fell most where they had been most common — the spatial face of [Wage Polarization](note:wage-polarization).
3. **Non-college city workers moved down, not up.** In dense places non-college adults shifted out of middle-skill jobs into low-skill service, transport and laborer jobs, not into high-skill ones.

4. **The urban wage premium for the less educated faded.** In 1970 wages rose with density for every education group; by 2015 the gradient had flattened for those without a high-school degree and steepened for post-college workers.
How has the "work of the past" — middle-skill urban jobs open to non-college workers — changed, and what does it imply for where and for whom opportunity is concentrated?

US Census 1970–2000 and pooled ACS 2014–2016 (IPUMS), with occupations harmonized across decades and mapped to 722 consistent [Commuting Zone](note:commuting-zone)s ordered by 1970 population density.

blocks.md: Values read off the charts are in [US Skill and Occupation Shifts by City Density 1970-2015](note:us-skill-and-occupation-shifts-by-city-density-1970-2015).

- Descriptive: the figures show where and for whom change happened, not why (automation, trade and offshoring are all candidates).
- Places are ordered by 1970 density, so the comparison is across places with different starting points, not a causal effect of density.

sections.heading: In Econ 424 L5 International Trade Empirics

blocks.md: The lecture asks "why start with regional analysis, other than identification?" and answers with these figures: something interesting is happening across space. They connect the inequality facts from earlier lectures (polarization, falling returns for the less educated) to geography, motivating the regional trade studies that follow.
